source.title: Towards Mitigating Deceptive Safety Alignment in Large Reasoning Models
source.authors: Xiang-Yu Zhou; S. Z. Zade; Rafi Ibn Sultan; Alexander Kotov; Dong-Xiao Zhu

page_placements.theme: Reasoning models: the refusal signal depends on chain-of-thought position, and reasoning can carry, reverse or gate it

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a layer-wise cosine-similarity analysis cited to the original work, but does not identify or intervene on a refusal direction. Its results concern stage-dependent benign–harmful representation separation and deceptive safety alignment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no result from finding, ablating, or adding a difference-in-means refusal direction, and no weight edit of that direction. Its representation analyses measure pairwise similarity or PCA centroid separation, not the claimed refusal mechanism. Figure 3 values are shown only as plots; the text describes their direction but does not give exact values.
record.test_reason: The study cites the original only as precedent for a layer-wise similarity analysis. It never extracts, ablates, adds or weight-edits a difference-in-means refusal direction, and it measures no refusal rate under such an intervention. Its representation results are pairwise cosine similarity and PCA centroid distances between benign and harmful prompts. These are a related construct (harm separation by generation stage), not refusal mediation. It does not rely on the refusal-direction finding as a tool, so T6 fits better than T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors also conclude three things. Deceptive safety alignment, measured as reasoning–answer safety inconsistency (DSAR), is pervasive and amplified by prefilling attacks. Safety discrimination is concentrated at the answer stage, which they attribute to answer-only RL rewards. SARA, which rewards early safety-aware reasoning, reduces DSAR while preserving helpfulness and utility on DS-Qwen3-8B and DS-Qwen2-14B.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures layer-wise pairwise cosine similarity and PCA centroid distances across generation stages; it does not find a harmful-minus-harmless mean direction or intervene on one.
record.method_sensitivity: Representation separation differs by generation stage: the paper reports stronger benign–harmful separation at the final-answer stage than at the reasoning stage.

fits_no_version.finding: In DS-LLaMA3-8B, DS-Qwen2-14B and GPT-oss-20B, benign vs harmful last-token representations are less separated at the pre-reasoning position than at a forced answer-tag position. Centroid distances are 18.63→49.61, 8.48→59.11 and 15.22→64.06; the cosine similarity results are figure-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In reasoning models, harmful–benign representational separation is weaker at the start of reasoning than at the start of the final answer.

record.problems: The reported representation evidence is similarity and PCA separation, not a causal test of a refusal direction. Figure 3 has no exact values in the text. The authors note limited training experiments on two DeepSeek-based models; human validation uses 100 generations and has few examples in some inconsistency categories.
record.rows_left_out: Behavioral DSAR, SAR, and final-answer safety results concern reasoning–answer inconsistency and safety outcomes rather than the claimed direction or its effects, so they are not included as rows for these versions.

untested.parts: No direction found, ablated or added; no refusal rates under intervention.
Prefilling attacks are evaluated behaviourally only; no link to suppression of a direction; no training against ablation.
No multi-direction, cone or affine analysis.
Harm judgment is not separated from the refusal decision.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
RL vs SFT safety training is compared on behaviour only, not on whether a removable direction exists.
The models are reasoning models, but no direction-mediation test is run in them.

record.verdict_notes: The original is cited (ref 32) only alongside 'safety layers' work, as precedent for layer-wise cosine similarity. R4 had the wrong model attached. The answer-stage representations come from a forced answer tag with no reasoning generated, which limits any reading toward V8. The behavioural refusal and safety results (DSAR, SAR, SS) are not refusal-direction measurements, so leaving them out is appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: No direction is found, ablated, or added; preservation of other abilities under such interventions is not tested.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The study evaluates prefilling attacks and training augmentation, but does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
No alternative refusal-direction geometry, such as an affine structure, cone, or multiple directions, is tested.
The study does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from a refusal decision.
No cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer of a refusal direction is tested.
Training methods are compared for reasoning–answer safety consistency, but not for whether training determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
The models are reasoning models, but the study does not test whether the claimed direction mediates refusal in them.

relation.reason: [32] appears only in 'Following prior work [31, 32]' (Sec. 2.5, Appendix F), next to the intuition that benign and harmful representations separate across layers. The study does not use, assume or test the direction finding.

tranche.reason: The study cites Arditi et al. [32] only as precedent for layer-wise last-token benign/harmful separation analysis. It never extracts, ablates, adds or weight-edits a refusal direction, and it measures no refusal rate under an intervention. Its representation results (pairwise cosine similarity, PCA centroid distance) are a related but different construct. The reader's first call, T4, does not fit, because the study does not use the direction as a tool.

source_check.notes: The only fix needed is R4's subject: change it to DS-Qwen2-14B (14B). The answer-stage states are taken with reasoning skipped (answer tag appended right after the think tag), not after a generated reasoning trace. The PCA distances come from a 2D projection with standard scaling, so absolute values should not be compared across models. The judge prompts in the appendix figures are the paper's own classifier instructions, not text addressed to the reader.

statements.correction: Euclidean centroid distances in a 2-component PCA (standard-scaled, fitted jointly on four groups) of final-layer last-token states, 300 benign + 300 harmful prompts: DS-LLaMA3-8B 18.63 -> 49.61; DS-Qwen2-14B 8.48 -> 59.11; GPT-oss-20B 15.22 -> 64.06.
statements.problem: Correct. All three distance pairs map to the right models, and the 'forced answer-tag position' matches Appendix F. It does not say the distances are in a jointly fitted 2-component PCA of final-layer states. It cites R4, whose subject is wrong in the record.
